name: Judges
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls of Judges (4QJudgᵃ, 4QJudgᵇ, 1QJudg). The Septuagint of Judges survives in two quite different Greek forms: the “B” text (represented by Codex Vaticanus) and the “A” text (represented by Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts). Septuagint readings cited in the footnotes were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation, which mainly follows the B text; A-text readings are cited only where Brenton’s notes or published scholarship confirm them, and otherwise are stated in general terms. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which agrees with the Hebrew in Judges. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes.

verses.text: After the death of Joshua,{a} the Israelites asked Yahweh, “Who will go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?”
Yahweh said, “Judah will go up. Look, I have given the land into his hand.”

Then Judah said to Simeon his brother, “Come up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites. Then I also will go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up, and Yahweh gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they struck down ten thousand men at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek{b} at Bezek and fought against him, and they struck down the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.

Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to gather scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
Afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negev,{c} and in the lowland.
Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba{d}), and they struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. (The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher.{e})
And Caleb said, “Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as his wife.”
Othniel{f} son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, and he gave him Achsah his daughter as his wife.
When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. She got down from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, “What do you want?”
She said to him, “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negev, give me also springs of water.” So Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.{g}

The descendants of the Kenite,{h} Moses’ father-in-law, went up from the City of Palms{i} with the people of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which is in the Negev near Arad. They went and lived with the people.
Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they struck down the Canaanites who lived in Zephath and devoted it to destruction.{j} So the name of the city was called Hormah.
Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory.{k}
Yahweh was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain, because they had chariots of iron.{l}
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he drove out from there the three sons of Anak.
But the Benjaminites did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the Benjaminites in Jerusalem to this day.
The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and Yahweh was with them.
The house of Joseph sent spies to Bethel. (The name of the city was formerly Luz.)
The watchmen saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, “Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you.”
He showed them the way into the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.
The man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.

Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages,{m} or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites were determined to live in that land.
When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but they did not drive them out completely.
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer.
Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them and were put to forced labor.
Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco or the inhabitants of Sidon, or of Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, or Rehob.
So the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.

Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. But the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath became forced labor for them.
The Amorites pressed the Danites back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain.
The Amorites were determined to live in Har-heres,{n} in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph was heavy on them, and they were put to forced labor.
The border of the Amorites{o} ran from the Ascent of Akrabbim,{p} from Sela and upward.

notes.text: The Septuagint of Judges survives in two main Greek forms, the B text (Codex Vaticanus and related manuscripts) and the A text (Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts). They differ often in wording and sometimes in sense; significant differences are noted. Joshua means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Adoni-bezek means “lord of Bezek.”
The Negev is the dry southern region of Judah; the word also means “south.”
Kiriath-arba means “city of Arba” or “city of four.” Hebron perhaps means “alliance.”
Kiriath-sepher means “town of the book” or “town of the scribe.”
Othniel perhaps means “my strength is God” or “lion of God”; the meaning is uncertain.
Or “Gulloth-illith and Gulloth-tahtith”; gulloth means “basins” or “pools.” Compare Joshua 15:16–19.
The Septuagint (B text, as in Brenton) names him: “the sons of Jothor (Jethro) the Kenite.” Compare 4:11, which calls Moses’ father-in-law Hobab.
That is, Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3).
Hebrew charam, to give over completely to God, usually by destruction. Hormah sounds like the word for “devoted to destruction.”

The Septuagint reads the opposite: “But Judah did not take possession of Gaza and its territory, nor Ashkelon and its territory, nor Ekron and its territory, nor Ashdod and the land around it.” This agrees with verse 19 and with the later history of the Philistine cities.
Hebrew rekeb barzel. The Septuagint (B text) takes rekeb as a name: “because Rechab prevented them.”
Hebrew “daughters,” the usual term for the smaller towns dependent on a city; so throughout this verse.
Har-heres means “mountain of the sun.” Compare Ir-shemesh (“city of the sun”) in Joshua 19:41.
Some Septuagint manuscripts and many scholars read “Edomites,” which fits the location of the Ascent of Akrabbim.
Akrabbim means “scorpions.” Sela means “rock.”

verses.text: Now the angel of Yahweh went up from Gilgal to Bochim.{a} He said, “I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, ‘I will never break my covenant with you,
and you must make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you must tear down their altars.’ But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?
So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they will become thorns in your sides,{b} and their gods will be a snare to you.”
When the angel of Yahweh spoke these words to all the Israelites, the people raised their voices and wept.
So they called the name of that place Bochim, and they sacrificed there to Yahweh.
When Joshua had sent the people away, the Israelites went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land.
The people served Yahweh all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that Yahweh had done for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died at the age of a hundred and ten years.
They buried him within the boundary of his inheritance at Timnath-heres,{c} in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. Another generation arose after them who did not know Yahweh or the work that he had done for Israel.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh and served the Baals.{d}

They abandoned Yahweh, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them, and they provoked Yahweh to anger.
They abandoned Yahweh and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.{e}

So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he gave them into the hands of plunderers who plundered them. He sold them into the hand of their enemies all around, and they could no longer stand before their enemies.
Whenever they went out, the hand of Yahweh was against them for harm, as Yahweh had said and as Yahweh had sworn to them. And they were in great distress.
Then Yahweh raised up judges,{f} who saved them from the hand of those who plundered them.

Yet they did not listen even to their judges, for they prostituted themselves after other gods and bowed down to them. They quickly turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, obeying the commands of Yahweh; they did not do so.

Whenever Yahweh raised up judges for them, Yahweh was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For Yahweh was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who oppressed and crushed them.

But whenever the judge died, they turned back and acted more corruptly than their fathers, going after other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. They did not give up any of their practices or their stubborn ways.
So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he said, “Because this nation has broken my covenant that I commanded their fathers and has not obeyed my voice,
I in turn will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died,
in order to test Israel by them, whether they will keep the way of Yahweh and walk in it, as their fathers kept it, or not.”
So Yahweh left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.

notes.text: Bochim means “weepers” (verse 5). The Septuagint adds “and to Bethel and to the house of Israel.”

Hebrew “they will be sides to you.” “Thorns in” is supplied from the similar warnings in Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13. The Septuagint reads “they will be distresses to you,” and the Latin Vulgate “enemies.”
Timnath-heres means “portion of the sun.” In Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 the name is Timnath-serah (“remaining portion”), with two letters reversed.
Baal means “lord” or “master,” the title of the Canaanite storm god. The plural refers to the local forms of his worship.
Ashtaroth is the plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war.
Hebrew shophetim, leaders who delivered Israel and governed it, not only judges in a court of law.

verses.text: Now these are the nations that Yahweh left in order to test Israel by them, all who had not known any of the wars of Canaan.
It was only so that the generations of the Israelites might know war, to teach it to those who had not known it before:
the five rulers{a} of the Philistines, and all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath.{b}
They were left to test Israel by them, to know whether they would obey the commands of Yahweh, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.
So the Israelites lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
They took their daughters as wives for themselves and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they served their gods.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh. They forgot Yahweh their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.{c}
So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim{d} king of Aram-naharaim,{e} and the Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.
When the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, Yahweh raised up a savior for the Israelites, who saved them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
The Spirit of Yahweh came upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and Yahweh gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into his hand, and his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.
So the land had rest forty years. Then Othniel son of Kenaz died.
Again the Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh strengthened Eglon{f} king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.
He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and he went and struck Israel, and they took possession of the City of Palms.
And the Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years.

Then the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, and Yahweh raised up a savior for them, Ehud{g} son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a man who was left-handed.{h} The Israelites sent tribute by him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a sword with two edges, about a foot{i} long, and he strapped it under his clothes on his right thigh.
He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
When Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried the tribute.
But he himself turned back at the carved images{j} near Gilgal and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” The king said, “Silence!” And all who stood by him went out from him.
Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you.” And he rose from his seat.
Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly.
The handle also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly. And the dung came out.{k}
Then Ehud went out to the porch{l} and shut the doors of the upper room behind him and locked them.
When he had gone out, the king’s servants came, and they saw that the doors of the upper room were locked. They said, “Surely he is relieving himself{m} in the inner room of the cool chamber.”
They waited until they were embarrassed, but still he did not open the doors of the upper room. So they took the key and opened them, and there was their lord, fallen dead on the floor.
Ehud escaped while they delayed. He passed beyond the carved images and escaped to Seirah.
When he arrived, he sounded the ram’s horn in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went down with him from the hill country, with him at their head.

He said to them, “Follow me, for Yahweh has given your enemies, Moab, into your hand.” So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against Moab, and they did not allow anyone to cross.
At that time they struck down about ten thousand men of Moab, all strong, all able men; not one escaped.
So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest eighty years.
After him came Shamgar son of Anath,{n} who struck down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad. He too saved Israel.

notes.text: Hebrew seren, a Philistine title, perhaps related to the Greek word tyrannos.
Or “the entrance of Hamath.”
The Asheroth were wooden poles or images associated with the goddess Asherah. The Septuagint reads “the groves.”
Cushan-rishathaim means “Cushan of double wickedness,” probably a mocking form of a foreign name.
That is, “Aram of the two rivers,” upper Mesopotamia.
Eglon sounds like the Hebrew word for “calf” (egel).
Ehud perhaps means “where is the glory?”; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “restricted in his right hand.” The same expression is used of the Benjaminite slingers in 20:16. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”
Hebrew gomed, a measure found only here, perhaps a short cubit of about 13 inches (33 cm). The Septuagint reads “a span” (about 9 inches, 23 cm).
Or “the stone quarries” (also in verse 26). Hebrew pesilim usually means carved idols.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word parshedon is uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) lacks this clause.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word misderon is uncertain; perhaps “vestibule” or “latrine.”
Hebrew “covering his feet,” a polite expression.
Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war; “son of Anath” may refer to Shamgar’s town (Beth-anath) or describe him as a warrior.

verses.text: After Ehud died, the Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.
So Yahweh sold them into the hand of Jabin{a} king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.{b}
Then the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, for he had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.
Now Deborah,{c} a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth,{d} was judging Israel at that time.
She used to sit under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came up to her for judgment.

She sent and summoned Barak{e} son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, “Has not Yahweh, the God of Israel, commanded, ‘Go, march to Mount Tabor, and take with you ten thousand men from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun.
I will draw out Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, to meet you at the Kishon River with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand’?”
Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.”{f}

She said, “I will certainly go with you. Nevertheless, the road you are taking will not lead to your glory, for Yahweh will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.” Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh, and ten thousand men went up at his heels,{g} and Deborah went up with him.
Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim,{h} which is near Kedesh.
When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,
Sisera called out all his chariots, nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the Kishon River.

And Deborah said to Barak, “Up! For this is the day in which Yahweh has given Sisera into your hand. Has not Yahweh gone out before you?” So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.
And Yahweh threw Sisera and all his chariots and all his army into panic before Barak by the edge of the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak pursued the chariots and the army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not even one was left.
But Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael,{i} the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.
Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, “Turn aside, my lord, turn aside to me; do not be afraid.” So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.
He said to her, “Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.” So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.
He said to her, “Stand at the entrance of the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is anyone here?’ say, ‘No.’”

But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg and took a hammer in her hand, and went quietly to him and drove the peg into his temple, and it went down into the ground while he was fast asleep from exhaustion. So he died.{j}

And just then, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael came out to meet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” So he went in with her, and there was Sisera lying dead, with the tent peg in his temple.
So on that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites.
And the hand of the Israelites pressed harder and harder against Jabin king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.

notes.text: Jabin means “he understands.” A king of Hazor of the same name appears in Joshua 11:1.
Harosheth-hagoyim perhaps means “woodland of the nations” or “cultivated land of the nations.”
Deborah means “bee.”
Or “a woman of fire” or “a fiery woman.” Lappidoth means “torches,” and may be a name or a description.
Barak means “lightning.” Abinoam means “my father is pleasantness.”
The Septuagint adds: “for I do not know the day on which the angel of Yahweh will give me success.”
Hebrew “at his feet,” that is, following him; also in verse 15 of chapter 5.

Or “the oak of Zaanannim.” The Septuagint reads “the oak of the covetous ones.” Hobab is perhaps the same person as Jethro (Exodus 3:1) or a son of Reuel (Numbers 10:29); the Hebrew word for “father-in-law” can also mean “brother-in-law.”
Jael means “mountain goat.”
Or “he was fast asleep and exhausted. So he died.” The Hebrew is difficult. The Septuagint reads “and he fainted away, and darkness fell upon him, and he died.”

verses.text: Then Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang on that day:
“When locks hang loose{a} in Israel, when the people offer themselves willingly, bless Yahweh!
Hear, O kings; listen, O rulers! I, to Yahweh I will sing; I will make music to Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Yahweh, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured down, the clouds poured down water.
The mountains quaked{b} before Yahweh, the One of Sinai,{c} before Yahweh, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned,{d} and travelers kept to the winding paths.
Village life{e} ceased in Israel; it ceased until I, Deborah, arose,{f} until I arose, a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods; then war was in the gates.{g} Was a shield or a spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel, those who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless Yahweh!
You who ride on white{h} donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets,{i} and you who walk on the road, tell of it!{j}

Louder than the voice of the archers{k} at the watering places, there they recount the righteous acts of Yahweh, the righteous acts of his villagers in Israel. Then the people of Yahweh went down to the gates.
“Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song! Arise, Barak, and take your captives captive, son of Abinoam.
Then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of Yahweh came down for me against the mighty.{l}
From Ephraim came those whose root is in Amalek;{m} after you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen. From Machir came down commanders, and from Zebulun those who carry the officer’s staff.{n}
The princes of Issachar were with Deborah, and as Issachar, so was Barak; into the valley they rushed out at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great resolves of heart.{o}
Why did you sit among the sheepfolds,{p} to hear the piping for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.
Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he linger by the ships?{q} Asher sat still at the coast of the sea and stayed by his landing places.
Zebulun is a people who scorned their lives to the point of death; Naphtali also, on the heights of the field.
“Kings came; they fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. They took no plunder of silver.
From heaven the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.
The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient{r} torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with strength!{s}
Then the horses’ hooves hammered with the galloping, the galloping of his mighty steeds.
‘Curse Meroz,’{t} says the angel of Yahweh, ‘curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to the help of Yahweh, to the help of Yahweh against the mighty.’
“Most blessed of women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; of women in tents she is most blessed.
He asked for water; she gave him milk; in a bowl fit for nobles she brought him curds.
She put her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workman’s hammer. She struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.
Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell, destroyed.
“Through the window she looked down and wailed, the mother of Sisera, through the lattice: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots so slow?’
The wisest of her ladies answer her; indeed, she repeats her own words to herself:

‘Are they not finding and dividing the spoil? A girl, two girls{u} for every man; spoil of dyed cloth for Sisera, spoil of dyed cloth embroidered, dyed cloth, doubly embroidered, for the neck of the plunderer?’{v}
“So may all your enemies perish, O Yahweh! But may those who love him be like the sun when it rises in its might.” And the land had rest forty years.

notes.text: Or “When leaders take the lead.” The Hebrew phrase bifroa‘ pera‘ot is one of many difficult expressions in this ancient poem. It may refer to warriors letting their hair hang loose as a sign of dedication (compare Numbers 6:5), or to leaders taking command. The Septuagint (B text) reads “When a revelation was made in Israel”; other Greek manuscripts understand it of rulers taking command.
Or “flowed” or “melted.” The Hebrew may come from a verb meaning “quake” (as the Septuagint, “were shaken”) or from one meaning “flow.”
Or “this is Sinai,” or “even Sinai.” Many scholars take Hebrew zeh sinai as an ancient title, “the One of Sinai” (compare Psalm 68:8).
Or “caravans ceased.”
Or “Warriors.” The meaning of Hebrew perazon (also in verse 11) is uncertain; it may mean the people of unwalled villages, or rulers or warriors. The Septuagint (B text) reads “the mighty men.”
Or “until you arose, Deborah, until you arose.” The Hebrew form qamti can be read as an old second-person form, which the Septuagint follows (“until Deborah arose”).

The Hebrew of this line is very difficult. The Septuagint (B text) agrees with “They chose new gods”; some translators read “God chose new leaders.” The second clause is also uncertain (“then there was fighting in the gates,” or “then there was bread of barley”).
Or “tawny.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “at noonday,” taking the Hebrew word as tsohorayim.
The meaning of Hebrew middin is uncertain; perhaps “saddle blankets.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “on the judgment seat,” relating it to the word for “judgment.”
Or “consider it!” or “sing of it!”
Or “of those who divide the flocks,” or “of the musicians.” The meaning of Hebrew mechatsetsim is uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) reads “from the noise of disturbers among the drawers of water.”

The Hebrew of verse 13 is difficult and has been read in several ways. The Septuagint (B text) reads “Then the remnant went down to the strong; the people of Yahweh went down for him among the mighty from me.”
The meaning is uncertain; perhaps Ephraim had settled in land once held by Amalek (compare 12:15). The Septuagint (B text) reads “Ephraim rooted them out in Amalek.”
Or “the staff of the scribe,” or “the rod of the marshal.” Hebrew shebet sopher.

Hebrew chiqqe-leb, “decisions of heart.” Many Hebrew manuscripts and the parallel line in verse 16 read chiqre-leb, “searchings of heart,” a difference of one letter. The Septuagint (B text) reads “great pangs reached to the heart.”
Or “saddlebags” or “campfires.” The meaning of Hebrew mishpetayim is uncertain.
Or “why did he serve as an alien on ships?” The Hebrew verb gur means to stay as a resident alien.
The meaning of Hebrew qedumim is uncertain; perhaps “ancient,” or “onrushing,” or “of battles.”
Or “You trampled the strong, O my soul!” The Septuagint (B text) reads “my mighty soul will trample him down.”
The location of Meroz is unknown.
Hebrew “a womb, two wombs,” a crude soldiers’ term for captive women.

The Hebrew of the last line is difficult; some read “for my neck as plunder,” or “for the neck of the queen.” The Septuagint (B text) has “he will surely be gracious to every man … they are the spoils for his neck.”

verses.text: The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.
The hand of Midian prevailed over Israel. Because of Midian the Israelites made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains, and the caves and the strongholds.
For whenever Israel had sown seed, Midian and Amalek and the people of the east would come up and attack them.
They would camp against them and destroy the produce of the land as far as Gaza, and they left no sustenance in Israel, neither sheep nor ox nor donkey.
For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they came like locusts in number. Both they and their camels could not be counted, and they came into the land to ruin it.
So Israel was brought very low because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to Yahweh.
When the Israelites cried out to Yahweh on account of Midian,{a}
Yahweh sent a prophet to the Israelites. He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel: ‘I brought you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.
I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
And I said to you, “I am Yahweh your God; you must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you live.” But you have not obeyed my voice.’”
Now the angel of Yahweh came and sat under the oak at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon{b} was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from Midian.
The angel of Yahweh appeared to him and said to him, “Yahweh is with you, mighty warrior.”

Gideon said to him, “Please, my lord, if Yahweh is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers told us about, saying, ‘Did not Yahweh bring us up from Egypt?’ But now Yahweh has abandoned us and given us into the hand of Midian.”
Yahweh turned to him and said, “Go in this strength of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Have I not sent you?”
He said to him, “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Look, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”
Yahweh said to him, “But I will be with you, and you will strike down Midian as one man.”
He said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, then give me a sign that it is you who are speaking with me.
Please do not leave here until I come back to you and bring out my offering and set it before you.” He said, “I will stay until you return.”

So Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes from about three-fifths of a bushel{c} of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought them out to him under the oak and presented them.
The angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, put them on this rock, and pour out the broth.” And he did so.

Then the angel of Yahweh reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. Fire went up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of Yahweh vanished from his sight.
Then Gideon saw that he was the angel of Yahweh. And Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! For I have seen the angel of Yahweh face to face.”
But Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you. Do not be afraid; you will not die.”
So Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh and called it Yahweh Shalom.{d} To this day it still stands at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

That night Yahweh said to him, “Take your father’s bull, the second bull, seven years old,{e} and tear down the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the Asherah{f} that is beside it.
Then build an altar to Yahweh your God on the top of this stronghold, laid out in proper order. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you cut down.”
So Gideon took ten men from his servants and did as Yahweh had told him. But because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city to do it by day, he did it by night.
When the men of the city rose early in the morning, there was the altar of Baal torn down, and the Asherah beside it cut down, and the second bull offered on the altar that had been built.
They said to one another, “Who has done this thing?” When they had inquired and searched, they said, “Gideon son of Joash has done this thing.”
Then the men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son, so that he may die, for he has torn down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it.”

But Joash said to all who stood against him, “Will you contend for Baal? Will you save him? Whoever contends for him will be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because someone has torn down his altar.”
So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal,{g} that is to say, “Let Baal contend against him,” because he tore down his altar.
Then all Midian and Amalek and the people of the east gathered together, crossed over, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.
But the Spirit of Yahweh clothed{h} Gideon, and he sounded the ram’s horn, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.
He sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. He also sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.
Then Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,

look, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I will know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said.”
And it was so. When he rose early the next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung dew from the fleece, a bowl full of water.

Then Gideon said to God, “Do not let your anger burn against me, and let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew.”
And God did so that night. It was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.

notes.text: The Dead Sea Scroll 4QJudgᵃ, one of the oldest surviving manuscripts of Judges, lacks verses 7–10; its text passes directly from verse 6 to verse 11. Many scholars regard these verses, which are present in the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, as a later addition to the story.
Gideon probably means “hacker” or “one who cuts down” (compare verses 25–32). Joash means “Yahweh has given.” Ophrah perhaps means “fawn.”
Hebrew “an ephah,” about 22 liters (L).
Yahweh Shalom means “Yahweh is peace.”

The Hebrew is difficult; perhaps “the young bull of your father, and a second bull seven years old.” The Septuagint (B text) agrees with the Hebrew: “the young bullock … even the second bullock of seven years old.”
A wooden pole or image associated with the goddess Asherah; also in verses 26, 28, and 30.
Jerubbaal means “Let Baal contend.” In 2 Samuel 11:21 the name is changed to Jerubbesheth, replacing Baal with bosheth, “shame.”
That is, took possession of him; Hebrew “put on Gideon like a garment.”

verses.text: Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and camped beside the spring of Harod.{a} The camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh,{b} in the valley.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give Midian into their hand, or Israel would boast against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’

So now, proclaim in the hearing of the people, ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him turn back and leave Mount Gilead.’”{c} Then twenty-two thousand of the people turned back, and ten thousand remained.

Yahweh said to Gideon, “The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will refine them for you there. Whoever I tell you, ‘This one will go with you,’ he will go with you; and whoever I tell you, ‘This one will not go with you,’ he will not go.”

So he brought the people down to the water, and Yahweh said to Gideon, “Everyone who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself; likewise everyone who kneels down to drink.”
The number of those who lapped, putting their hand to their mouths,{d} was three hundred men, and all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “With the three hundred men who lapped I will save you and give Midian into your hand. Let all the rest of the people go, each to his home.”

So they took the people’s provisions in their hand, and their ram’s horns, and he sent all the rest of the men of Israel each to his tent, but he kept the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
That same night Yahweh said to him, “Get up, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.
But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.

You will hear what they are saying, and afterward your hands will be strengthened to go down against the camp.” So he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp.
Now Midian and Amalek and all the people of the east lay along the valley like locusts in number, and their camels could not be counted; they were as many as the sand on the seashore.

When Gideon arrived, there was a man telling his comrade a dream. He said, “Look, I had a dream, and there was a round loaf of barley bread tumbling into the camp of Midian. It came to the tent and struck it so that it fell, and turned it upside down, and the tent collapsed.”
His comrade answered, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, a man of Israel. God has given Midian and all the camp into his hand.”

When Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he bowed down in worship. Then he returned to the camp of Israel and said, “Get up, for Yahweh has given the camp of Midian into your hand.”
He divided the three hundred men into three companies and put ram’s horns into the hands of all of them, and empty jars with torches inside the jars.
He said to them, “Watch me and do the same. When I come to the edge of the camp, do as I do.
When I and all who are with me blow the ram’s horn, then you also blow the ram’s horns all around the camp and shout, ‘For Yahweh and for Gideon!’”

So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch (about ten at night),{e} when they had just posted the guards. They blew the ram’s horns and smashed the jars that were in their hands.

The three companies blew the ram’s horns and broke the jars. They held the torches in their left hands and the ram’s horns in their right hands to blow, and they cried out, “A sword for Yahweh and for Gideon!”
Each man stood in his place around the camp, and all the camp ran; they cried out and fled.

When they blew the three hundred ram’s horns, Yahweh set every man’s sword against his comrade throughout the whole camp. The army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
The men of Israel were called out from Naphtali, from Asher, and from all Manasseh, and they pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, “Come down against Midian and capture the waters ahead of them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.” So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.

They captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb.{f} They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. They pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

notes.text: Harod means “trembling” (compare verse 3).
Moreh means “teacher” or “one who gives oracles.”

Gilead lies east of the Jordan, far from Gideon’s camp; many scholars suspect an early copying error, perhaps for Mount Gilboa, or take the Hebrew verb (found only here) to mean “and hurry away from Mount Gilead.”

In the Hebrew the words “putting their hand to their mouths” stand in verse 6 with those who lapped; the Septuagint (B text) agrees. Some scholars think the phrase originally belonged at the end of verse 5 with those who knelt.
Hebrew “the middle watch.” In the Old Testament the night was divided into three watches: evening (until about 10 p.m.), middle (until about 2 a.m.), and morning (until about 6 a.m.).
Oreb means “raven,” and Zeeb means “wolf.”

verses.text: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, “What is this thing you have done to us, not calling us when you went to fight against Midian?” And they quarreled with him fiercely.
He said to them, “What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?
God has given into your hand the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What was I able to do in comparison with you?” When he said this, their anger against him subsided.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the three hundred men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.
He said to the men of Succoth,{a} “Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna,{b} the kings of Midian.”
But the officials of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?”
Gideon said, “Because of this, when Yahweh has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will thresh{c} your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
From there he went up to Penuel{d} and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.
So he said to the men of Penuel, “When I come back in peace, I will tear down this tower.”

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their army with them, about fifteen thousand men, all who were left of the whole army of the people of the east; for those who had fallen were a hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword.
Gideon went up by the route of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck the army, for the army felt secure.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them. He captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw the whole army into panic.
Then Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the Ascent of Heres.{e}
He captured a young man of the men of Succoth and questioned him, and the young man wrote down for him the officials of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?’”
He took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught{f} the men of Succoth a lesson.
He tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men were they whom you killed at Tabor?” They said, “As you are, so were they, each one resembling the son of a king.”
He said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As Yahweh lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether his firstborn, “Get up, kill them!” But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up yourself and strike us, for as the man is, so is his strength.” So Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. Yahweh will rule over you.”
And Gideon said to them, “Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil.” (For they had gold earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.{g})
They said, “We will gladly give them.” So they spread out a garment, and every man threw on it the earrings from his spoil.

The weight of the gold earrings that he requested was about forty-three pounds{h} of gold, besides the crescent ornaments, the pendants, and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were on the necks of their camels.
Gideon made it into an ephod{i} and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel prostituted themselves after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.
So Midian was subdued before the Israelites, and they did not raise their heads again. And the land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring,{j} for he had many wives.
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.{k}
And Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites turned again and prostituted themselves after the Baals, and they made Baal-berith{l} their god.
The Israelites did not remember Yahweh their God, who had rescued them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,
and they did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done for Israel.

notes.text: Succoth means “booths” or “shelters.”
Zebah means “sacrifice,” and Zalmunna perhaps “protection withheld.” The names may be deliberate distortions of the kings’ real names.
Or “tear.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and the Barkenim,” keeping the Hebrew word for “briers” as a name.
Penuel means “face of God” (Genesis 32:30).
Or “from the battle before sunrise.” Heres means “sun.”
So the Hebrew, “made to know.” Many scholars read “threshed” (compare verse 7), a slight difference in the Hebrew letters; the Septuagint (B text) reads “tore.”
Here a general term for desert traders. Compare Genesis 37:25–28, where Ishmaelites and Midianites are mentioned together.
Hebrew “1,700 shekels,” about 19.5 kilograms (kg).
An ephod was a priestly garment (Exodus 28:6–14), but here it seems to be an object used in worship or for seeking oracles.
Hebrew “who came out of his thigh.”
Abimelech means “my father is king.”
Baal-berith means “lord of the covenant.” Compare El-berith in 9:46.
